exercise1.prompt: Turning a measurement into a band you can count.

hiddenCases.name: the boundaries land in the right band
a perfect score is still an A
the bottom of the range is an F

exercise1.hint: cut with edges at -1, 69, 79, 89 and 100 puts each boundary score in the band above it, because the right-hand edge belongs to its band.

questions.explain: It converts a continuous measurement into a category you can count and group by.

questions.prompt: With the default right=True, which band does a value equal to an edge fall into?
questions.explain: The right-hand edge belongs to its own band, so a score of 89 with an edge at 89 is in the band that ends there. Getting this backwards moves everyone on a boundary.

questions.prompt: Why does binning make the boundary decision explicit?
choices: You have to write the edges down, so the choice is visible and reviewable
questions.explain: A grade boundary buried in a chain of if statements is a decision nobody can find later. The bins list is that decision, written once.
